after.worked_solution:
Using the fact that $4=\frac{4}{1},$ we can write the expression as

$$
\frac{4}{1}-\frac{(-2)}{q}=.
$$

 

In order to subtract the two fractions, we need them to have a common denominator. So, we put both fractions over a common denominator of $q$ by multiplying the top and bottom of the first fraction by $q:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{4}{1}-\frac{(-2)}{q} & = \\ \frac{q}{q}\cdot \frac{4}{1}-\frac{(-2)}{q} & = \\ \frac{4q}{q}-\frac{(-2)}{q}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we subtract the fractions and simplify the result:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{4q}{q}-\frac{(-2)}{q} & = \\ \frac{4q-(-2)}{q} & = \\ \frac{4q+2}{q} & = \\ \frac{2(2q+1)}{q}\end{aligned}
$$

a
2wz−4w−3(z−1)(2w−3)
b
2wz−3(z−1)(2w−3)
c

decision.explanation: Using the common denominator (z-1)(2w-3), the numerator is (2w-3)+2w(z-1)=2w-3+2wz-2w=2wz-3. Thus option b is correct.

after.name: Question 3
after.worked_solution:
In this case, we need to put the fractions over a common denominator of $(z-1)(2w-3),$ since there are no common factors in either denominator that we can exploit. 

To do this, we multiply the top and bottom of the first fraction by $2w-3,$ and the top and bottom of the second fraction by $z-1:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{z-1}+\frac{2w}{2w-3} & = \\ \frac{2w-3}{2w-3}\cdot \frac{1}{z-1}+\frac{z-1}{z-1}\cdot \frac{2w}{2w-3} & = \\ \frac{2w-3}{(z-1)(2w-3)}+\frac{(z-1)2w}{(z-1)(2w-3)} & = \\ \frac{(2w-3)+(z-1)2w}{(z-1)(2w-3)} & = \\ \frac{2w-3+2wz-2w}{(z-1)(2w-3)} & = \\ \frac{2wz-3}{(z-1)(2w-3)}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\frac{3}{1}+\frac{5-p}{p}.
$$

 

In order to add the two fractions, we need them to have a common denominator. So, we put both fractions over a common denominator of $p$ by multiplying the top and bottom of the first fraction by $p:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{1}+\frac{5-p}{p} & = \\ \frac{p}{p}\cdot \frac{3}{1}+\frac{5-p}{p} & = \\ \frac{3p}{p}+\frac{5-p}{p}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we add the fractions and simplify the result:

$$
